The whole book translated from the Greek Septuagint, printed under USFM code ESG. It carries the Catholic canon's Greek additions but not the Vulgate's chapter numbers for them: the translators merged the five additions into the Hebrew chapter numbering as extensions of 1:1 and of 3:13, 4:17, 8:12 and 10:3, so this Esther has ten chapters and the Vulgate's Esther 11-16 do not exist here at all. A roman-1962 citation of Esther 13 or 14 therefore finds no chapter and refuses, which is correct. Chapter 10 runs to 14 verses against the Vulgate's 13, and its 10:4, “Mordecai said, These things have come from God”, is the Vulgate's 10:4; no calendar tracked here cites inside that addition, so no correspondence is asserted for the rest of it. Verses 4:6, 9:5 and 9:30 are absent from this text, the Greek carrying no matter at those numbers.

edition_title: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
note: Deuterocanonical, and in the Catholic canon. TRAP: “Eccli.” is this book, not Ecclesiastes. This edition follows the Greek, whose chapter and verse division differs from the Vulgate throughout and often by several verses: 1359 verses here against the Douay-Rheims's 1591. The postconciliar Lectionary numbers Sirach from the Greek and its citations therefore address this edition correctly; the 1962 Missal numbers it from the Vulgate and its citations do not. Both calendars cite 36:18 for the introit Da pacem Domine, and that verse stands here at 36:16; the verse-alias table carries the correspondence, which was established by reading the verse and not by an offset. This edition also omits verses the Vulgate carries, marking each with an editorial note that it is omitted by the best authorities: 1:5, 1:7, 1:21, 3:19, 10:21, 11:15-16, 13:14, 16:15-16, 17:5, 17:9, 17:16, 17:18, 17:21, 18:3, 19:18-19, 19:21, 20:3, 22:9-10, 24:18, 24:24, 25:12 and 26:19-27. Those numbers are absent from this text, not merged into a neighbour, and a citation of them refuses for want of the verse.

Deuterocanonical, and in the Catholic canon. Chapter 6 is the Epistle of Jeremias, as in the Vulgate, and the book has the same 213 verses as the Douay-Rheims but not the same division: this edition joins the Vulgate's 3:34 and 3:35 into one verse, so from 3:35 to the end its verse stands one behind the number a Vulgate citation means, chapter 3 ends at 37 where the Vulgate ends at 38, and the Vulgate's “Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men” is this edition's 3:37. WARNING: a citation of a single verse in 3:35-3:37 resolves here to the verse after the one it means. It is deliberately not withheld in the verse-alias table, because the only reading either tracked calendar makes of this passage is the Easter Vigil's Baruch 3:9-15, 32-4:4, whose range covers the same words under either numbering and which withholding rows would break; the Vulgate's 3:38 cited alone falls past the end of the chapter and refuses.

edition_title: The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions
note: The whole book translated with its Greek portions, printed under USFM code DAG. It carries the Catholic canon's three Greek additions inside Daniel as the Vulgate does — the Prayer of Azarias and the Canticle of the Three Children in chapter 3, Susanna as chapter 13 and Bel and the Dragon as chapter 14 — so it has the Vulgate's fourteen chapters. Its verse division inside those additions is the Greek one and not the Vulgate's: chapter 3 has 97 verses against the Vulgate's 100 and chapter 13 has 64 against 65, and the divergence is not a uniform offset. It was measured verse by verse. Chapter 3 agrees with the Vulgate from 3:24 to 3:51 and again from 3:79 to 3:97, and does not correspond between 3:52 and 3:78, where the Greek and the Vulgate order and divide the Canticle of the Three Children differently; that whole span is withheld in the verse-alias table. The Vulgate's 3:98-100 do not exist here, the Greek numbering them 4:1-3, and a citation of them refuses for want of the verses.
